title: Computer Architecture
objectives: Reason about the memory hierarchy and why caches matter
Use locality of reference to write faster code

sections.markdown: Computer architecture is the set of rules and structures describing how a computer's hardware (CPU, memory, I/O) is organized and how it cooperates to execute instructions.

## Why it exists
Software does not run on magic — it runs on silicon. Understanding the machine explains **why caches matter**, why memory layout affects speed, and why concurrency is hard. Interviewers probe this to see if you understand performance from first principles.

Think of a **kitchen**: the CPU is the chef, RAM is the countertop (fast but small), the SSD is the pantry (large but slower), registers are the chef's hands, and cache is the small shelf beside the stove. A good chef keeps what they need closest.

## Internal working — the cycle
The CPU repeats four steps billions of times per second:
- **Fetch** the next instruction (address in the Program Counter)
- **Decode** what it means
- **Execute** it in the ALU
- **Write-back** the result; advance the PC

sections.code:
[ CPU ]
  Registers   ~1 cycle      (fastest, tiny)
  L1 cache    ~4 cycles
  L2 cache    ~12 cycles
  L3 cache    ~40 cycles
[ RAM ]       ~100-300 cycles
[ SSD ]       ~10,000+ cycles
[ Network ]   millions of cycles

sections.markdown: **Locality of reference** is the #1 performance lever. Temporal = reuse data soon; spatial = use nearby data. Arrays beat linked lists in practice because contiguous memory is cache-friendly.
Beginners assume '1 line of code = 1 unit of time'. A cache miss can cost 100x more than an arithmetic op. Always think about data layout.
Senior engineers reason in **cache lines** (~64 bytes). Struct-of-arrays often beats array-of-structs for hot loops because it packs the hot fields together.

flashcards.front: What are the 4 stages of the CPU cycle?

flashcards.back: CPU registers (~1 cycle), then L1/L2/L3 cache, then RAM.
Temporal: reuse the same data soon. Spatial: access nearby data. Both make caches effective.
Code and data share one memory bus, so the CPU can stall waiting on memory — the 'memory wall'.

quiz.q: Which storage is the fastest for the CPU to access?
quiz.explain: Registers sit inside the CPU and take ~1 cycle — faster than any cache or RAM.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the instruction cycle?
quiz.explain: The CPU fetches, decodes, executes, then writes back the result.

quiz.q: Why are arrays often faster than linked lists despite similar Big-O?
quiz.explain: Arrays store elements contiguously, so cache lines bring in neighbors — great spatial locality.

quiz.q: A cache miss compared to an arithmetic operation is roughly…
quiz.explain: Going to main memory on a miss can cost ~100x an in-register op — why data layout matters.
